title: “5 Practices for Orchestrating Productive Mathematics Discussions” can help you improve student dialogues and learning ns-can-help-you-improve-student-dialogues-and-learning/
author: Mary Resanovich
summary: Mary Resanovich of NWEA reviews Margaret Smith and Mary Kay Stein's book on orchestrating productive mathematics discussions. She traces the shift from teacher-led demonstration to the communication standards in NCTM documents and the Common Core, and cites research showing that rich dialogue and explanation raise achievement, including for lower-performing students. The book's five practices are anticipating, monitoring, selecting, sequencing, and connecting, all aimed at using student thinking as the launching point for discussion. She stresses the two steps that come first, defining a learning goal that states mathematical understanding rather than a procedural performance goal and choosing a task of high cognitive demand. Resanovich says the power of the framework lies in the planning it encourages, which she wishes she had done as a teacher, so discussion becomes intentional rather than left to chance.
points: Research links rich mathematical dialogue, including explaining alternative strategies, to higher achievement across student groups.
The five practices are anticipating, monitoring, selecting, sequencing, and connecting, and they make discussion purposeful rather than recitation.
A learning goal should state what students understand about mathematics, which is richer than a procedural performance goal.
Task selection matters, and tasks can be modified to push beyond calculating an answer toward generalizing patterns.
The framework's value lies in pre-planning follow-up questions, which students present, and in what order.
quotes: Explaining their thinking helps students clarify, and sometimes revise, their thinking.
Therefore, discourse needs to be planned with these goals in mind, not merely as a ‘checking for understanding’ form of recitation.

Teachers often think of lessons in relation to the activities that they will ask students to do rather than what students will come to know and understand about mathematics as a result of having engaged in the lesson.

The goal of using these practices is to come into a lesson and discussion as prepared as possible to guide the conversation toward attainment of the lesson goals and greater conceptual understanding of math.

This framework ensures students are not just conversing for the sake of conversing, but that their dialogue is being purposefully sequenced and facilitated to enrich learning of both the lesson goals and math in general.

When I taught, I often took the time to consider what misconceptions or common errors my students might produce. However, I did not think about follow-up questions I might ask based on these misconceptions or errors.

Ultimately, the goal is not simply to get students talking more, but to engage them in the kinds of mathematical conversations that deepen understanding, build confidence, and help them all see themselves as capable mathematicians.
